CA-03.001: earth is a rocky planet with surface oceans and an atmosphere. below the crust and mostly solid mantle lie a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. as earth rotates, most locations periodically move through light and shadow. earth's rotational axis is tilted relative to the perpendicular to its orbital plane. as the planet travels around the sun, each hemisphere receives different amounts of sunlight at different times of year. geographic coordinates are conventions; the planet itself provides physical reference features. atmosphere rotation
CA-03.002: water moves among the ocean, atmosphere, soil, organisms, rivers, lakes and ice. evaporation transfers water from a liquid surface to water vapor. cooling can produce droplets or ice in clouds. precipitation can return water to the surface, where some runs into rivers or seeps into the ground. near standard atmospheric pressure of 101,325 pascals, pure water freezes near 273 kelvin and boils near 373 kelvin. changing pressure changes the temperature at which it boils. dissolved material can also shift freezing and boiling behavior. these are examples of how the same substance changes form. the rounded temperatures describe pure water near equilibrium. a picture of a cloud shows droplets or ice rather than gaseous water vapor. evaporation precipitation
CA-03.003: sunlight delivers energy to earth. the surface and atmosphere absorb part of it, and the earth system emits energy to space largely as infrared radiation. water moving through the atmosphere and ocean can redistribute energy between different regions. weather describes atmospheric conditions on short timescales. climate describes patterns such as typical temperatures and precipitation, and how variable they are over much longer intervals. a storm image records one event. a collection of measured conditions over many years supports judgments about a changing pattern. climate and geology interact at the surface. rain and ice can weather rock and carry sediment. the movement of tectonic plates can build relief and change the surface that winds and water flow across. a picture, such as the hurricane image, can document an event without establishing a long-term trend. different questions about climate require different geographical and time scales. weather climate
CA-03.004: water is distributed across earth's ocean, inland water bodies, ice, atmosphere, soil and underground spaces. a reservoir can retain water for very different durations depending on its location and the mechanisms moving water into and out of it. water can enter the atmosphere from surfaces or plants, return as precipitation, infiltrate the ground, or flow through rivers toward other reservoirs. solar heating and gravity help drive these transfers. a diagram of the cycle describes recurring processes rather than a single path that every molecule follows. a global conceptual diagram cannot describe local water availability, contamination or changes through time. reservoir infiltration
CA-03.005: earth's rigid outer layer, the lithosphere, includes the crust and uppermost mantle. it is broken into plates that move relative to one another. where plates separate at ocean ridges, hot material can rise and form new crust. at some convergent boundaries one plate descends into the mantle beneath another. at transform boundaries plates move past one another. patterns of earthquakes, volcanic activity and magnetic stripes on the ocean floor support this model. instruments can also measure the motion of locations on earth's surface over time. satellites can observe surface forms such as the east african rift, where parts of the lithosphere are being pulled apart. surface shape alone does not establish the motion or whether a nearby earthquake is imminent. plate boundaries can be wide or complex. lithosphere subduction
CA-03.006: the ocean and atmosphere exchange energy and matter across their boundary. winds can drive surface currents. differences in water temperature and salinity affect density and help drive deeper movements. currents redistribute heat across an otherwise unevenly heated planet. when water evaporates, it takes energy from its surroundings. water vapor carries this energy and can release energy during condensation. observing wind, surface temperature and humidity together helps investigators estimate exchanges that cannot be read from a single photograph. ocean and atmosphere interactions occur at different time and length scales. currents and individual cloud patterns can vary with depth, season and location. salinity current
CA-03.007: weathering breaks down or alters material in place. water can react with minerals, and expanding ice can force open cracks. erosion moves material by water, wind, ice or gravity. when the transporting flow loses the capacity to carry some particles, those particles may accumulate as sediment. soils develop from parent material affected by climate, organisms, relief and time. they can contain minerals, organic material, water and air. soil layers can differ in composition and structure. burrowing, roots, decomposition and movement of water help change them over time. landscape photographs illustrate surface forms. soil composition, formation time and rates of erosion need local measurements or geological evidence. weathering erosion
